propositions.text: I dismiss this appeal.
propositions.quote: I dismiss this appeal.

paragraphs.summary: The court dismisses this appeal.

propositions.text: The Appellant is a Bangladeshi citizen fearing persecution by Awami League and Chatra League for opposing extortion and refusing to hand over father's business.
propositions.quote: The Appellant, XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX, is a citizen of Bangladesh. He fears persecution in Bangladesh at the hands of the Awami League (AL) and the Chatra League (CL) due to his opposition to their extortion attempts and his refusal to hand over his father's business.

propositions.text: In 2017, local CL leader demanded subscription payment; refusal led to threats against Appellant's family and police refused to act properly.
propositions.quote: In XXXX 2017, a local CL leader demanded the Appellant's father pay XXXX lakh as a "subscription". When his father refused, five or six CL "goons" came to the Appellant's home and threatened his mother. When the Appellant and his father returned home, they were also threatened. They attempted to report the situation to police, but the police told them to remove the name of the CL members from their complaint.

propositions.text: Appellant continued to receive threats and left Bangladesh to study in Canada to escape at father's insistence.
propositions.quote: The Appellant continued to receive threats and, at the insistence of his father, left Bangladesh and came to study in Canada as a means to escape.

paragraphs.summary: The court states the Appellant is a Bangladeshi citizen fearing persecution by AL and CL for opposing extortion; threats occurred and police refused proper help; Appellant fled to Canada.

propositions.text: The Appellant arrived in Canada in 2018 and filed refugee claim in January 2020.
propositions.quote: The Appellant arrived in Canada on XXXX XXXX 2018. He filed his claim for refugee protection on 27 January 2020.

paragraphs.summary: The court states the Appellant arrived in Canada in 2018 and filed refugee claim in January 2020.

propositions.text: The RPD found discrepancies between Appellant's narrative, documents, and testimony, concluding he was not credible on balance of probabilities.
propositions.quote: The RPD found that due to discrepancies between the Appellant's Basis of Claim (BOC) narrative, his documents, and his testimony, the Appellant was, on a balance of probabilities, not credible.

propositions.text: The RPD found the credibility finding determinative of the Appellant's claim.
propositions.quote: It found this was determinative of the Appellant's claim.

paragraphs.summary: The RPD found the Appellant not credible due to discrepancies and this was determinative of his claim.

propositions.text: The Appellant argues the RPD breached natural justice or procedural fairness and that credibility findings are erroneous.
propositions.quote: In essence, he argues that the RPD breached natural justice or procedural fairness. He also argues that the RPD's credibility findings are erroneous.

propositions.text: The Appellant's submissions lack precision and clarity.
propositions.quote: The Appellant's submissions lack precision and clarity.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the Appellant's submissions lack clarity; the Appellant argues RPD breached natural justice and erred on credibility.

propositions.text: Evidence can be accepted only if it arose after RPD decision, was not reasonably available then, or could not reasonably have been brought before RPD.
propositions.quote: According to the Law,1 I can only accept evidence that: (i) arose after the RPD decision; or (ii) was not reasonably available at the time of the decision; or (iii) that the Appellant could not reasonably have been expected in the circumstances to bring to the RPD before the decision.

paragraphs.summary: The court states the legal test for accepting new evidence after the RPD decision.

propositions.text: If evidence meets requirements, it must be new, credible, and relevant to be accepted.
propositions.quote: If the evidence meets one or more of these requirements, I must decide if the evidence is new, credible, and relevant before I can accept it.

paragraphs.summary: The court states new evidence must be new, credible, and relevant to be accepted.

propositions.text: The Appellant asks to admit recent US Department of State Country Report on Bangladesh.
propositions.quote: The Appellant asks that I admit the most recent United States Department of State's Country Report on Human Rights Practices for Bangladesh.

propositions.text: The court finds no need to admit the document as it is already in the National Documentation Package for Bangladesh.
propositions.quote: I find there is no need to enter this document as it is already included in the most recent National Documentation Package (NDP) for Bangladesh.

paragraphs.summary: The Appellant requests admission of a US report; the court finds it unnecessary as it is already in the National Documentation Package.

propositions.text: No new evidence admitted; no jurisdiction to hold oral hearing.
propositions.quote: As no new evidence has been admitted, I have no jurisdiction to hold an oral hearing.

paragraphs.summary: The court states no new evidence admitted and thus no jurisdiction for oral hearing.

propositions.text: The court's role is to review all evidence and decide if RPD made the correct decision.
propositions.quote: My role is to look at all the evidence and decide if the RPD made the correct decision.

paragraphs.summary: The court states its role is to review all evidence and decide if RPD decision was correct.

propositions.text: The Appellant alleges RPD was biased, aggressive, lacked knowledge of Bangladesh conditions, and failed to consider guidelines, COVID-19, and Appellant's condition.
propositions.quote: The Appellant argues that the RPD was biased, was aggressive in its questioning, and did not have sufficient knowledge of country conditions in Bangladesh. He argues the RPD failed to consider the chairperson's guidelines, the COVID-19 situation and the stress, psychological and emotional condition of the Appellant in assessing his claim.

paragraphs.summary: The Appellant alleges RPD bias, aggressive questioning, lack of knowledge, and failure to consider guidelines, COVID-19, and his condition.

propositions.text: No evidence of RPD bias, aggressive questioning, or disregard of Appellant's circumstances found after review of record and audio.
propositions.quote: I find no evidence of bias or of inappropriately aggressive questioning or tone of the part of the RPD nor its disregard of the Appellant's particular circumstances.

propositions.text: RPD identified credibility issues and gave Appellant opportunity to respond.
propositions.quote: On the contrary, I find the RPD clearly identified the credibility issues and provided the Appellant with an opportunity to respond to its concerns.

propositions.text: Some RPD questions were direct and pointed but not inappropriate.
propositions.quote: Although some of its questions were direct and pointed,

paragraphs.summary: The court finds no RPD bias or inappropriate questioning; RPD identified credibility issues and allowed Appellant to respond.

propositions.text: Chairperson's Guideline defines vulnerable persons as those severely impaired in presenting cases, requiring special procedural consideration.
propositions.quote: The Guideline defines vulnerable persons as follows: 2. Definition of vulnerable persons 2.1 For the purposes of this guideline, vulnerable persons are individuals whose ability to present their cases before the IRB is severely impaired.

propositions.text: The Guideline applies to refugee claimants, appellants, and persons concerned before IRB, including close family members in some cases.
propositions.quote: 2.2 The definition of vulnerable persons may apply to persons presenting a case before the IRB, namely, to refugee protection claimants (in the RPD), appellants (in the IAD and in the RAD), and persons concerned (in the ID).

propositions.text: IRB proceedings recognize vulnerabilities but Guideline addresses severe cases needing special procedural handling.
propositions.quote: It is intended to apply to individuals who face particular difficulty and who require special consideration in the procedural handling of their cases. It applies to the more severe cases of vulnerability.

propositions.text: Vulnerability must be supported by independent credible evidence where reasonably possible.
propositions.quote: Wherever it is reasonably possible, the vulnerability must be supported by independent credible evidence filed with the IRB Registry.

paragraphs.summary: The court explains Chairperson's Guideline defining vulnerable persons as severely impaired individuals needing special procedural consideration, supported by credible evidence.

propositions.text: No evidence shows Appellant is severely impaired or needs special consideration beyond RPD procedures.
propositions.quote: I see no evidence to show that the Appellant is severely impaired or that he requires special consideration beyond that which is already inherent in the RPD's procedures.

propositions.text: Appellant's counsel asserts COVID-19 prevented psychological and emotional medical assessment.
propositions.quote: Due to Covid 19 the claimant could not do the psychological and emotional medical assessment of her (sic) present medical condition,

propositions.text: No basis found for COVID-19 impairment claim; Appellant was represented and understood questions at hearing.
propositions.quote: I find no basis for this submission. The Appellant was represented at his hearing and did not indicate that his ability to provide evidence was in any way impaired.

propositions.text: Appellant's answers were understandable though unsatisfactory; no evidence of impairment or denial of natural justice.
propositions.quote: Although his answers may not have been satisfactory, this alone is not evidence either of an impairment or a denial of natural justice.

propositions.text: Appellant's counsel made written submissions after hearing without raising medical or psychological impairment needing special consideration.
propositions.quote: Further, the Appellant's counsel provided submissions in writing subsequent to the hearing and did not raise any medical, psychological or other impairment which required special consideration.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds no evidence Appellant is severely impaired or needs special consideration; COVID-19 claim unsupported; Appellant understood hearing questions.

propositions.text: The Appellant's natural justice arguments are rejected.
propositions.quote: The Appellant's arguments with respect to natural justice are therefore rejected.

paragraphs.summary: The court rejects the Appellant's natural justice arguments.

propositions.text: The Appellant asserts RPD's credibility findings are incorrect but provides no specific errors.
propositions.quote: The Appellant asserts that the RPD's credibility findings are incorrect. Again, counsel for the Appellant does not point to any specific errors.

propositions.text: Appellant's counsel outlines general principles without applying them to case facts or evidence.
propositions.quote: Rather, he outlines several general principles without applying them to the facts or evidence of this case.

paragraphs.summary: The Appellant asserts RPD credibility findings are incorrect but offers no specific errors, only general principles unlinked to facts.

propositions.text: RAD is not to argue for Appellant but reviewed RPD's credibility findings due to inadequate submissions.
propositions.quote: It is not for the Refugee Appeal Division (RAD) to make arguments for the Appellant. However, given the inadequacy of the arguments submitted by counsel on the Appellant's behalf, I have found it necessary to consider each of the RPD's credibility findings to determine whether they are correct.

propositions.text: While disagreeing with some RPD findings, overall RPD did not err in negative credibility assessment or assigning little weight to documentation.
propositions.quote: While I disagree with some of the RPD's findings, I find that, overall, it did not err in its negative assessment of the Appellant's credibility or in assigning little weight to his documentation.

paragraphs.summary: The court notes RAD is not to argue for Appellant but reviewed RPD findings and finds overall no error in negative credibility assessment.

propositions.text: RPD found involvement of Minister S. in attacks was speculative.
propositions.quote: The RPD first found that the involvement of Minister S. in the attacks against the Appellant and his family was speculative.

propositions.text: The court agrees with RPD that Minister S.'s involvement is speculative and no evidence of government or AL involvement exists.
propositions.quote: I agree. The Appellant's testimony was that in order for the agents of persecution to be able to attack the Appellant's house and business, they would need the support of a powerful person. The RPD did not err in finding this was speculative. Aside from this, there was no evidence of Minister S.'s, or any other government or AL, involvement.

paragraphs.summary: The court agrees with RPD that Minister S.'s involvement in attacks is speculative and unsupported by evidence.

propositions.text: Appellant testified mother fainted and he was injured in 2017 attack; medical report provided for his clinic visit.
propositions.quote: With respect to the attack on XXXX XXXX 2017, the Appellant testified that, "... my mother became unconscious and we took her to the hospital and I also had sustained cut injuries on my back after they beat me up with iron rods, so I also went to the clinic. My entire body had lot of blood marks and bruises because of the beating." The Appellant provided a medical report to document his trip to the clinic.

propositions.text: Appellant's BOC stated mother fainted due to hypertension and they were busy caring for her; no mention of his clinic visit.
propositions.quote: However, the Appellant's BOC indicates that, "My mother could not bear the trauma and she fainted due to hypertension. So, we immediately brought her to a nearby hospital for treatment and became busy taking care of her."

propositions.text: RPD asked why Appellant omitted his clinic visit from BOC; Appellant said he did not know how it was omitted.
propositions.quote: The RPD asked him why he had not mentioned that he had been treated at the clinic as well. The Appellant responded, "Yes, I clearly remember that I had stated in my narrative that I had to go to the clinic. I don't know how that part got omitted from the narrative."

paragraphs.summary: The RPD found Appellant's testimony about his clinic visit omitted from BOC and inadequately explained.

propositions.text: The court finds the omission of Appellant's clinic visit from BOC is a minor inconsistency but agrees RPD found it inadequately explained.
propositions.quote: Although I find this is a relatively minor inconsistency, I agree with the RPD's finding that it was not adequately explained.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the omission of Appellant's clinic visit is minor but inadequately explained, agreeing with RPD.

propositions.text: Short delay between last incident and departure is not fatal to claim
propositions.quote: I agree with the RPD that the short delay between the last incident on XXXX XXXX 2018 and the Appellant's departure from Bangladesh on XXXX XXXX 2018 is not fatal to his claim.

propositions.text: No adverse inference from appellant hiding at home because RPD did not ask why he hid there
propositions.quote: I draw no adverse inference from the fact that the Appellant hid at his home during this period. This is because the RPD did not ask him to explain why he hid at home rather than hiding somewhere else.

propositions.text: RPD's findings about police phone number availability are speculative
propositions.quote: Findings with regard to availability of phone number for the police are speculative

paragraphs.summary: Court agrees short delay is not fatal, rejects adverse inference about hiding at home, finds police phone number findings speculative.

propositions.text: RPD erred in drawing negative inference from appellant not calling police during 2017 attack
propositions.quote: I find the RPD erred in drawing a negative inference from the fact that the Appellant had not called the police during the XXXX 2017 attack.

propositions.text: RPD's finding that police number was easily available is speculative given documentation showing no emergency number then
propositions.quote: RPD's finding that the number for the local police station was easily available is speculative in light of the documentation which shows there was no emergency number for the police at the relevant time.

paragraphs.summary: Court finds RPD erred in negative inference about not calling police, as police number availability was speculative.

propositions.text: RPD erred in drawing negative inference from omission of conversation with agent of persecution in 2018 attack
propositions.quote: I also find the RPD erred in drawing a negative inference from the Appellant's omission of a conversation with the agent of persecution that occurred at the time of the XXXX XXXX 2018 attack.

propositions.text: Narrative shows more than a one-line verbal exchange; no obvious inconsistencies found
propositions.quote: I find it is clear from the narrative that there was more than a "one-line verbal exchange". While the Appellant provided more detail in testimony, I see no obvious inconsistencies.

propositions.text: No adverse inference drawn on this point
propositions.quote: I draw no adverse inference on this particular point.

paragraphs.summary: Court finds RPD erred in negative inference about omitted conversation; no inconsistencies found; no adverse inference drawn.

propositions.text: RPD correctly gave no weight to medical documents from 2018 assault due to vagueness
propositions.quote: I find the RPD correctly determined that these documents were too vague to be given any weight.

paragraphs.summary: Court agrees RPD correctly gave no weight to vague 2018 medical documents.

propositions.text: RPD correctly noted complainant's statement and FIR do not identify agent of persecution as complainant
propositions.quote: RPD correctly noted that the complainant's statement and the First Information Report (FIR) do not identify the agent of persecution as the complainant.

propositions.text: RPD correctly rejected appellant's explanation for knowing agent of persecution involved and drew negative inference
propositions.quote: I find no error in the RPD rejecting this explanation and drawing a negative inference with respect to the FIR.

paragraphs.summary: Court finds RPD correctly noted complainant and FIR do not identify agent, and properly rejected appellant's explanation.

propositions.text: RPD correctly found appellant's lawyer's letter lacked expected details
propositions.quote: I also agree with the RPD that the Appellant's lawyer's letter is lacking in details that could reasonably be expected.

propositions.text: RPD correctly noted appellant's lack of knowledge about charges undermined credibility
propositions.quote: The RPD correctly determined that these issues undermined the credibility of the Appellant's allegations.

paragraphs.summary: Court agrees RPD correctly found lawyer's letter lacking details and appellant's knowledge gaps undermined credibility.

propositions.text: RPD drew negative inference from absence of letter from appellant's father
propositions.quote: The RPD drew a further negative inference as the Appellant had not provided a letter from his father.

propositions.text: Appellant explained not wanting to burden father but did not explain why letter request was problematic
propositions.quote: The Appellant explained that he did not want to ask his father or add to his problems by asking for a letter. However, the Appellant did not explain why asking for a letter would pose such a problem.

propositions.text: Appellant obtained other documents from father, so RPD did not err in negative inference
propositions.quote: Particularly, since the Appellant did obtain other documents from his father such as his father's complaint to the police. The RPD did not err in this regard.

paragraphs.summary: Court finds RPD properly drew negative inference from no letter from father, given appellant's unexplained reluctance and other documents obtained.

propositions.text: RPD correctly noted supporting affidavits were hearsay, not firsthand witnesses
propositions.quote: The RPD correctly noted that none of the affiants who had provided supporting affidavits had witnessed any of the alleged events firsthand.

propositions.text: Affidavit of AO contradicts FIR filed by appellant's father
propositions.quote: Further, the affidavit of AO indicates that the police refused to take a complaint which directly contradicts the FIR filed by the Appellant's father.

paragraphs.summary: Court agrees RPD correctly noted affidavits were hearsay and found contradictions between affidavit and FIR.

propositions.text: Medical report from 2017 does not link assault to appellant's father or government extortion
propositions.quote: Even accepting this report at face value, there is nothing which links this assault to the Appellant's father or to extortion by government agents.

paragraphs.summary: Court finds 2017 medical report does not link assault to appellant's father or government extortion.

propositions.text: Letter from President alleging government involvement in attacks on appellant's father unsupported by evidence
propositions.quote: Statements contained in this letter - specifically that the government, Members of Parliament and Ministers are involved in the attacks on the Appellant's father - are simply not supported by any evidence.

paragraphs.summary: Court finds letter alleging government involvement in attacks on appellant's father unsupported by evidence.

propositions.text: None of the documentation can be given any weight
propositions.quote: I find that none of this documentation can be given any weight.

paragraphs.summary: Court finds none of the documentation can be given any weight.

propositions.text: Appellant failed to establish core allegations on balance of probabilities, fatal to claim under IRPA sections 96 or 97
propositions.quote: I find that the Appellant failed to establish, on a balance of probabilities, the core allegations upon which his claim is based. This is fatal to his claim whether considered under section 96 or 97 of Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA).

propositions.text: Appeal is rejected
propositions.quote: I therefore reject this appeal.

paragraphs.summary: Court concludes appellant failed to prove core allegations, rejects appeal under IRPA sections 96 or 97.

propositions.text: Appeal dismissed and RPD decision confirmed that appellant is not a Convention refugee or person in need of protection
propositions.quote: Pursuant to paragraph 111(1)(a), I dismiss the appeal and confirm the decision of the RPD that the Appellant is neither a Convention refugee nor a person in need of protection.

paragraphs.summary: Court dismisses appeal and confirms RPD decision appellant is not a refugee or person in need of protection.
